I'm wary that the recovery timing is ambiguous since both reverts happened close together — the monthly-spend-feature revert at 11:20:35 and the legacy-checkout-fallback revert at 11:22:46, with recovery observed at 11:23, so the causal attribution to legacy-checkout-fallback could actually be confounded by the earlier revert.

But I'm also noticing a wrinkle: if monthly-spend-feature's revert was judged refuted and then rolled back (flag turned on again), the flag could have been active again at recovery time, which would undercut the ZeroDivisionError theory tied to it unless the timing of that rollback is later than 11:23. I need to pin down the exact sequence of when each flag was on/off relative to the 11:23 recovery to make an honest causal claim.

The duration and impact numbers (9 minutes, 29.4% avg error rate, 36.5% peak, 28.3pp excess over baseline) are given by the shop's data, so I should cite them as measured rather than present them as my own calculation. As for whether the human lead changed what was done, it didn't shape the first action taken, but it did surface the legacy-checkout-fallback flag as the second candidate — which turned out to be the one confirmed as mitigation, so its influence was real even if indirect.

input.executive_summary: For about nine minutes on 11 October 2026 (11:14–11:23 UTC), the online shop's account page failed for a large share of shoppers. Over that stretch roughly three in ten requests returned an error, against a normal rate of about one in a hundred, with the worst minute near 36.5%; the measured excess over normal was 28.3% of traffic. The cause was a configuration switch changed in production, not new code — no release went out in that window. The on-call automation was paged at 11:19, spent the following minutes reading metrics, change history and logs, and then turned two recently changed switches back to their previous settings in sequence. After the second change the error rate returned to normal and the page stopped firing at 11:24. The service is currently in its recovered state, and a draft code change has been opened to remove the underlying fault in the account-page spend summary so the behaviour cannot recur if the switch is turned on again. Which of the two switches actually ended the outage is not settled by the evidence; the log detail and the sequence of actions disagree, and that should be resolved before the switch is re-enabled.

lead_effects.effect: The automated investigation formally marked this lead refuted on the log evidence (the legacy flag's only visible effect was pre-existing low-rate ClientDisconnected errors), but it still changed what was done: the flag it named was carried as the second candidate and was the subject of the second revert, which is the action credited with recovery and the one left in place.

input.root_cause: Not conclusively established. The log evidence points at the feature flag `monthly-spend-feature`: it rolled out across io-shop between 11:14 and 11:15, exactly at onset, and from that minute onward the account-page failures are `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47`, a code path that flag enables; no deploy or code change landed in the window, and the only other error type (`ClientDisconnected`) was present at low rate before and after the toggle. However, the automated verification contradicts this: reverting `monthly-spend-feature` did not restore the service within the 120s observation window and was undone, and recovery was only observed one minute after the second flag, `legacy-checkout-fallback`, was turned back on — with `monthly-spend-feature` on again at that point. Either the first revert worked but was judged too early (per-minute metric lag) and then wrongly undone, or the account-page breakage depended on both flags together; the available data does not separate those.
